conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were brought in after a seizure. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… my partner found me on the floor between the bed and nightstand. I don’t remember it. Then 30 minutes later, I had another one—full convulsions. I was confused after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had a similar episode about three weeks ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I was twitching, foaming at the mouth. Woke up in the ambulance. No loss of bladder or biting my tongue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your records. At that time, your EEG showed some slowing in the left temporal lobe, which can be linked to seizures. But no anti-seizure meds were started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. They said it might be from the pain meds or my pancreatitis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And now, with two more episodes, we’re treating this as likely temporal lobe seizures. Your head CT was normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having smells that aren’t there—like burning rubber. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a common aura for temporal lobe seizures. It’s a warning sign before the seizure starts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know that. I thought it was just in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s real, and it helps us make the diagnosis. We’ve consulted neurology, and they agree. We’re going to start you on Keppra, an anti-seizure medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help. You haven’t had any since arriving, which is a good sign. We’ll keep you on it and follow up with neurology after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been in a lot of pain from my pancreatitis. It flared up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see. Your lipase is normal, but that can happen with chronic pancreatitis. We’re keeping you NPO for now—no food by mouth—except meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I not even have water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just small sips for now. We’re giving IV fluids and will restart your J-tube feeds soon. We’re also giving Dilaudid for pain through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. The pain is better than last time, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it controlled. We also gave you ketorolac for inflammation and promethazine for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been dry heaving a bit. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with pancreatitis flares, nausea is common. The promethazine should help. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back—everything looks stable. Your kidney and liver function are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any news on the seizure tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for an MRI today to look for any brain changes. The EEG from before showed left temporal slowing, but no active seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the MRI tell us why this is happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps rule out things like tumors or strokes. Most likely, it’ll be normal, and we’ll attribute the seizures to your medication use and pancreatitis stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking tramadol and lorazepam for pain and anxiety… could that trigger seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially tramadol in high doses. Your tox screen showed methadone too, which wasn’t prescribed. That increases seizure risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know methadone was in my system. I only take what my doctors prescribe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you may have been getting prescriptions from multiple pharmacies. It’s common with chronic pain. We need to get this under control to prevent more seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want the pain to stop. I don’t want to hurt myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re setting up a plan. We’ll meet with your partner, your PCP, and social work to create a safer medication plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI came back. No tumors, strokes, or signs of acute injury. There are some small white matter changes, likely from aging or blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And no signs of mesial temporal sclerosis, which is good. Your EEG also didn’t show active seizures, just that old slowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s really the meds and stress causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Sleep deprivation, pain, and polypharmacy—especially tramadol and benzos—are likely triggers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been seizure-free since admission, which is excellent. Your pain is improving, and you’ve tolerated small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had toast and applesauce. No nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re switching your Dilaudid from IV to oral. Once that’s stable, we’ll remove the femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to get rid of that line. It’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We met with your partner and your PCP. We all agree: all your meds will now be managed by your PCP only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll dispose of all extra medications at home. You’ll sign a pain medication agreement. And you’ll attend a partial psychiatric program for pain and depression management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about that, but I know I need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good step. You’ll continue on amitriptyline, mirtazapine, and sertraline for depression. But we’re stopping the butalbital for migraines—it can worsen things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your femoral line is out. No bleeding or infection. You’re walking well and eating regular meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. No pain, no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And no seizures. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go home with Keppra twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a 7-day supply of tramadol—50mg three times a day max. And lorazepam, 1mg twice a day as needed. No refills. You’ll record every dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I need more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then you’ll call your PCP or go to the ER. The goal is to avoid overuse. Neurology will switch you from Keppra to Lamictal later—it helps with both seizures and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last day. BP’s a bit high—146/103. We’ll keep you on clonidine and lisinopril. Your PCP may increase the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stress maybe? My family meeting is coming up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Try to stay calm. You’re doing well. Discharge papers are ready. Home health will help with meds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m scared but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Keep all your follow-ups: neurology, PCP, psych program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll sign the medication contract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care. Call if you have another seizure or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.
